chapters.file: ch17 - Charlie Kaufman, Philosophy, and the Small Screen.md
chapters.relation: Chambers reads Kaufman's TV sitcom Ned and Stacey through queer theory, arguing its marriage-of-convenience premise stages a critique of 'the normal.' Because Ned and Stacey only play at being husband and wife and never desire the romantic telos, the show troubles heteronormativity more than the openly gay Will & Grace, whose characters chase marriage and family. Chambers uses Butler's Lacanian notion of masquerade to claim there is no 'real' husband or wife beneath the role, only role-playing, and ties this to the philia (not eros) bond of the leads and to the masquerade running through Kaufman's films.

chapters.file: ch18 - The Instructive Impossibility of Being John Malkovich.md
chapters.relation: Hagberg treats Being John Malkovich as a refutation of the dualist fantasy that one could achieve transparent knowledge of another mind by occupying it. Through the film's four levels—Schwartz as spectator inside Malkovich, Lotte's transgender re-embodiment, Schwartz's puppeteering, and Malkovich falling into his own portal to the 'Malkovich, Malkovich' hell—he shows, via Jamesian relational sensation and Wittgenstein's private-language argument, that it is always still Schwartz who senses, so no one ever becomes Malkovich. The self-enclosed Malkovich world, where everyone can only say 'Malkovich,' dramatizes that selfhood is relationally emergent (Royce, Mead) and that experience is inviolably one's own (Margalit on remembered emotion).

chapters.file: ch19 - Part 3. Being in the World, Partially.md
ch20 - Living a Part Synecdoche, New York, Metaphor, and the Problem of Skepticism.md
chapters.relation: Deming argues that Caden Cotard's attempt to build a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse enacts a skepticism toward the givenness of life—the belief that reality can be denied and remade as art. Drawing on Cavell's claim that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' and Heidegger on world, earth, and dwelling, he shows the play traps Caden rather than freeing him: to represent the world is to be flung outside it. He invokes Wittgenstein's image of language as an ancient city one can never step outside of, and Baudrillard's simulacra (Caden even considers titling the play 'Simulacrum'), to explain why the literal doubling fails to yield the 'true self' Caden seeks.

chapters.file: ch21 - “There’s No More Watching” Artifice and Meaning in Synecdoche, New York and Adaptation.md
chapters.relation: Hill argues that Adaptation and Synecdoche, New York both dramatize artists (the character Charlie Kaufman and Caden Cotard) struggling to portray 'real life' through artifice, and that Kaufman achieves authenticity not through neorealist naturalism but through surrealism and fantasy. He distinguishes the existentialist sense of authenticity—living self-awarely and choosing outside a community's rules (via Macquarrie)—from cinematic realism, tracing Kaufman's fusion of inner and outer life to Fellini's 8½. The chapter reads Synecdoche as an unflinching, near-horror examination of what it costs to make honest art, concluding its buried message is that creation is meaningless unless shared.

chapters.file: ch22 - Human Nature and Freedom in Adaptation.md
chapters.relation: Ganssle uses Adaptation's four main characters to test Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence against Walker Percy's account of immanence and transcendence. Laroche, endlessly adaptable ('Done with fish'), embodies Sartrean radical freedom and pure immanence; Donald owns his love ('You are what you love, not what loves you') and lives without bad faith; Orlean and Charlie are paralyzed in bad faith, unable to choose. Ganssle contrasts Sartre's rejection of a fixed human nature (grounded in atheism, against Plato's and Augustine's Forms) with Percy's view that persons are unlike infinitely mutable orchids, arguing the film sides with Percy: the antiessentialist self is 'lost in the cosmos.'

Smith reads every Kaufman film as a farce about the self-defeating quest to 'become who you are,' with Synecdoche, New York as its culmination: Caden's MacArthur-funded attempt to represent all of life in a warehouse collapses into infinite regress because a representation of everything must contain itself. He frames Kaufman's films as Montaignean/Emersonian essays—fragmentary self-portraits—and argues the film's limits are death and language, since language always puts us at one remove from the life we already are. The transcendence it evokes is naturalistic, akin to Nietzsche's amor fati and Emerson's 'we are born to a whole': wholeness is not achieved but already possessed, and the hidden knowledge of it turns tragedy into farce.

chapters.file: ch24 - Nietzschean Themes in the Films of Charlie Kaufman.md
chapters.relation: Shaw argues Kaufman's films embody a Nietzschean 'Dionysian pessimism' organized around the will to power, eternal recurrence, perspectivism, and a bundle-theory of the self. He reads Being John Malkovich through the bundle self: personal identity is the dominant drive that acts, so Malkovich 'becomes' Lester/Mertin, the will that controls the vessel. Adaptation's Laroche voices Nietzsche's plastic power of forgetting, and Eternal Sunshine dramatizes eternal recurrence and amor fati as Joel and Clementine choose to repeat their doomed love. Synecdoche, New York, by contrast, Shaw judges a failure of passive nihilism—Caden as the fly who never leaves the bottle—deadening rather than life-affirming.

chapters.file: ch25 - Inconclusive Unscientific Postscript Late Remarks on Kierkegaard and Kaufman.md
chapters.relation: LaRocca pairs Kaufman with Kierkegaard on anxiety as the constitutive human condition—not worry but 'the dizziness of freedom,' the awareness of radical possibility. He argues both use pseudonymity and 'indirect communication' to distance author from work so the audience confronts its own individuality: Kierkegaard's Haufniensis/Climacus, Kaufman's Caden Cotard and the character 'Charlie Kaufman' in Adaptation. The chapter analyzes acting as inhabitation vs. impersonation (Being John Malkovich vs. The Talented Mr. Ripley), the diegesis/mimesis layering (Plato and Aristotle) of Kaufman's doubles and replicas, and repetition/recursion as the Kierkegaardian leap that love, like faith, demands—so 'the end is built into the beginning.'

holes.name: Stanley Cavell
holes.what: American philosopher known for work on film ontology, skepticism, and the acknowledgment of others.
holes.why: Chapter 20 builds its central argument on Cavell's claim that 'film is a moving image of skepticism' and his ontology of the moving image, but no matching philosopher slug exists in the taxonomy.

holes.name: Walker Percy
holes.what: American novelist and philosophical essayist who analyzed the self's placement in the world via immanence and transcendence in Lost in the Cosmos.
holes.why: Chapter 22 sets Percy's account of immanence/transcendence as the direct foil to Sartre and uses it to interpret every main character, but the taxonomy has no slug for Percy or his transcendence/immanence framework.
